title: Farr's cholera table: deaths by height
hook: Farr recorded each London district's height above the Thames in 1849. What did cholera do?

knows: cholera hit poor, crowded parts of Victorian London
doesNotKnow: how strongly it fell with height above the Thames in Farr's own table
that height and water supply went together, so the table cannot separate them

misconception: A pattern as strong as this in the record shows the cause.
objective: The learner can say that in Farr's 1849 table cholera deaths fell steeply with height (about 5 times fewer at 80 feet and up), and that because the low districts mostly drew central-Thames water, the table alone cannot say whether height or water mattered.

claims.text: Farr's table gives cholera deaths, population, height above the Thames high-water mark and water supply for 38 London districts in 1849.
claims.source: history-data.mjs: cholera, Cholera.csv, columns district, cholera_deaths, popn, elevation (feet above high water), water (Farr's tables; the HistData doc names Brigham et al. 2003 as its source, the brief cites Bingham et al. 2004). Copied into Demo.tsx as DISTRICTS by a node script.
claims.note: FC pass 39 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Re-derived in my own node script from the pinned file (history-data.mjs pins all hold; sha256 re-checked) and compared with the copied array in Demo.tsx (identical). Cholera.csv 38 districts; Demo.tsx DISTRICTS identical (deaths, popn, elevation, water). HistData doc (opened): 'deaths from cholera in 1849', 'elevation, in feet above the high water mark', 'water supply region'; Source: Bingham et al. (2004) Table 2. (The doc's own description also says 'Brigham et al. (2003)'; the Source section is the citation to use.)

claims.text: The 16 districts under 20 feet lost 92 per 10,000; the 4 at 80 feet or more lost 20, about 5 times fewer.
claims.source: history-cycle2-check.mjs section 20: pooled deaths / population x 10,000: under 20 ft 8,584 / 935,869 = 91.7 -> 92; 80 ft and up (St Pancras, Islington, Marylebone, Hampstead) 19.8 -> 20; ratio 4.6 -> 'about 5'. Demo.tsx computes the same; the question's 92 is also computed. Dots plot each district's own rate (deaths / popn x 10,000, rounded; equals the file's cholera_drate).
claims.note: FC pass 39 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Under 20 ft: 16 districts, 8,584 / 935,869 = 91.7 (92); 80 ft and up: 4 districts (St Pancras, Islington, Marylebone, Hampstead), 817 / 412,415 = 19.8 (20); ratio 4.63, 'about 5' (and 'about a fifth as many'). Every district's own rate rounds to the file's cholera_drate.

claims.text: 11 of the 16 low districts drew their water from the Thames between Battersea and Waterloo ("Thames, central" on the stage).
claims.source: history-cycle2-check.mjs section 20 (11 of 16 with water = Battersea). The level 'Battersea' means 'Thames, between Battersea and Waterloo Bridges' per the HistData Cholera documentation (opened 2026-10-14 by the builder from raw.githubusercontent.com); 'Kew' = 'Thames, at Kew and Hammersmith'; 'New River' = 'New River, Rivers Lea and Ravensbourne'.
claims.note: FC pass 39 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Low districts by water: Battersea 11, New River 4, Kew 1. Doc (opened): 'Thames, between Battersea and Waterloo Bridges' (central London).

claims.text: Height and water went together, so this table alone cannot say which mattered; within the central-Thames districts, deaths still fall with height (r = −0.68).
claims.source: history-cycle2-check.mjs section 20: within-supplier correlations of elevation and death rate: Battersea -0.68 (12 districts), New River -0.55, Kew -0.47. Demo.tsx computes the Battersea value (Pearson r on the rounded rates). Brief: the lesson never says water alone.
claims.note: FC pass 39 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Within-supplier Pearson r (elevation vs rounded rate): Battersea -0.680 (12 districts), New River -0.548, Kew -0.475.

claims.text: Where it stops: these are deaths registered in one year, district by district.
claims.source: history-data.mjs: cholera, HistData Cholera documentation (1849 deaths by registration district). Brief #20: no held source sentence; Farr's miasma theory is not used.
claims.note: FC pass 39 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Doc (opened): 'number of deaths registered from cholera in 1849', by London district.

recall.question: In a city, the low streets have both more illness and the oldest wells. From those two facts alone, what causes the illness?
recall.why: When two possible causes go together, a pattern with one of them cannot separate it from the other.
